Bhaashya Systems: What Goes in the Window?

A million-token model arrives, an engineering lead proposes deleting six months of work, and a client in Dubai asks a question about data segregation that nobody on the call can answer.

Section 1Bengaluru, Tuesday, 21 April 2026

The renewal decision was due on 30 April, and Devika Iyer had nine days. She was Director of Product at Bhaashya Systems, a nine-storey walk from the Indiranagar metro station, and the document open on her screen was not a product spec but a security questionnaire. Al Rahba Technology Services, a Dubai-headquartered IT services firm and Bhaashya's second-largest customer at ₹2.4 crore of annual contract value, had sent forty-one questions ahead of renewal. Question 29 read: "Describe how content belonging to other customers is segregated during AI processing. State whether such content can be present in the same model request as our content."

Devika knew the honest answer, and she did not like it. Since a design change in February, Bhaashya's product had been sending a large slice of its shared answer library into every model call — and that library contained material written for other clients. Nobody had intended a confidentiality problem. They had intended a simplification.

Section 2The company

Bhaashya Systems was founded in 2021 by two former management consultants who had spent a decade watching Indian IT services firms lose deals not on capability but on paperwork. Their product, BidDesk, helps a firm respond to requests for proposal. A typical enterprise RFP runs 180 pages and asks 340 discrete questions — about delivery methodology, security certifications, escalation matrices, GST registration, past performance in the buyer's sector. Historically a bid team of six spent eleven days assembling answers, mostly by hunting through old submissions. BidDesk ingests the RFP, matches each question against the firm's library of previously approved answers, drafts a response, and flags what genuinely needs a human.

Bhaashya's twenty-six customers are mid-tier Indian services firms and global capability centres — the kind of organisations that bid against Infosys, TCS and Wipro for the same contracts and cannot match their proposal desks head for head. Annual recurring revenue was ₹18 crore. The team was ninety-one people: engineering in Bengaluru and Pune, a designer in Berlin, a data scientist in Toronto, customer success in Singapore, and a sales head in New Jersey who had sold the Al Rahba account and referred to it, in every forecast call, as "the logo".

Section 3The situation

In January 2026 Bhaashya's model provider released a version with a one-million-token context window, up from 200,000. Karthik Subramanian, the engineering lead in Bengaluru, saw an opportunity. BidDesk's retrieval layer — the machinery that searched the answer library and selected the eight most relevant past answers for each question — was the most complained-about part of the system. When it fetched the wrong answers, the draft was wrong, and no one could tell from the output why. Two engineers in Pune spent most of their time on it.

Karthik's proposal was to stop selecting. The full library was 41,000 approved answers, roughly 7.4 million tokens, which still would not fit. But the last eighteen months of it — 820,000 tokens — would, alongside the 110,000-token RFP itself. Send the whole recent library on every call, let the model find what it needs, and delete the retrieval layer. The change shipped on 14 February as an experiment on four accounts and was quietly extended to all of them by early March.

Three things then happened. Shruti Kamath, the customer-success lead in Singapore, reported that clients had started calling the "Generate All" button unusable: on a full 340-question bid it now took just over twelve minutes, against ninety seconds before. Lena Fischer, the designer in Berlin, filed a note saying she could design a progress indicator but not a twelve-minute one, and that two clients had begun generating questions in small batches to avoid it. And Arjun Nair, the data scientist in Toronto, finished a 600-bid evaluation whose findings were more uncomfortable than the latency.

Section 4The people

Karthik Subramanian, engineering lead, Bengaluru. Nine years in search infrastructure before Bhaashya. He wants the retrieval layer deleted and his two Pune engineers moved to the ingestion pipeline, which is genuinely understaffed. His argument is that retrieval failures are silent and unfixable, whereas a long prompt at least contains the right answer somewhere.

Nikhil Ranade, staff engineer, Pune. Built the retrieval layer and is defensive about it, but his technical point is precise: selection is the only place in the system where Bhaashya can enforce which client's material enters a request. Delete it and the enforcement point disappears.

Arjun Nair, data scientist, Toronto. Ran the 600-bid evaluation. He is indifferent to the organisational politics and interested only in the position effect he measured, which he considers the most important finding of the quarter and which he has explained twice on calls that started at 8:30 p.m. India time and 11 a.m. his time.

Sanjay Kulkarni, sales head, New Jersey. Wants the phrase "one million token context" on the website by the next quarter and has already used it in two conversations. He also owns the Al Rahba renewal and reads question 29 as a procurement formality that a well-worded paragraph will satisfy.

Exhibit 2 is the exhibit Karthik put on the screen first, and it is the one Devika found least useful. At 1,450 bids a year across all customers, the three designs cost ₹57.3 lakh, ₹17.0 lakh and ₹11.7 lakh respectively. Against ₹18 crore of revenue, even the worst of them is under 3.2% — real money, worth having, but not a number that decides anything. Once caching was switched on, the gap between the two live options narrowed to ₹365 per bid. Cost, Devika concluded, was not her constraint. It was Arjun's exhibit that was.

Exhibit 3 says that the model does not attend evenly to a 930,000-token prompt. When the correct past answer happened to sit near the beginning or the end of the library slice, the draft used it 89% and 85% of the time. When it sat in the middle, that fell to 61%. Averaged across positions, the long-context design reused the correct answer 74% of the time against 88% for the retrieval design it replaced — a fourteen-point regression that had been invisible because nobody measured reuse; they measured whether a draft was produced.

Arjun added a second finding in a footnote that Devika thought should have been the headline. In 9% of drafts, the model had answered from a superseded entry — quoting a certification that had lapsed in 2024, or a delivery-centre headcount that predated a restructuring — because the library slice contained both the old and the new entry with nothing to mark which was current. The old retrieval layer had filtered on a validity flag. The new design sent everything and trusted the model to choose.

Exhibit 4 is the one that connects to question 29. Fifty-three per cent of the tokens Bhaashya was sending on every call were attributable to a specific end client. Because the library is shared across a customer's own bid history, Al Rahba's pricing rationale for a Sharjah logistics contract was sitting in the same request as an unrelated bid — and, in the multi-tenant configuration two smaller customers used, in requests belonging to a different Bhaashya customer altogether. Nikhil had raised this in a comment on the February pull request. The comment had three thumbs-up reactions and no reply.

Section 6The options

Option A — Commit to long context

Delete the retrieval layer, move the Pune engineers to ingestion, and market the million-token window as Sanjay wants. Fix the specific defects found: add validity flags as visible text, sort the library so recent entries land at the beginning and end of the prompt, and answer question 29 by moving every multi-tenant customer onto a single-tenant index. Upside: one less system, faster feature work, a clean marketing story. Cost: the twelve-minute wait remains, the fourteen-point reuse gap is addressed only by re-ordering, and the confidentiality answer is a promise about configuration rather than a mechanism.

Option B — Rebuild retrieval and reverse February

Return to selection, and invest the two Pune engineers in making it better: hybrid keyword-plus-semantic search, a re-ranking pass, and per-client scoping enforced at the index. Upside: restores 88% reuse and ninety-second generation, and gives a mechanical answer to question 29 — material a caller is not entitled to never enters the request. Cost: Karthik's objection stands, retrieval misses stay silent and hard to debug, and Bhaashya spends the next two quarters on infrastructure rather than on the ingestion backlog that is losing it deals in onboarding.

Option C — Tier the two designs by what a bid is worth

Make scoped retrieval the default path for all 340 questions. For the twenty or thirty questions a bid manager marks as strategically decisive — usually past-performance narratives and differentiators — run a second long-context pass over a client-scoped, validity-filtered slice, with caching on. Upside: normal generation returns to ninety seconds, the confidentiality mechanism is retained, and the long window is spent where a miss costs a deal. Cost: two paths to maintain, a new judgement call about which questions are decisive, and a product surface that is harder to explain than either pure option.

Section 7Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly changed on 14 February, in terms of what the model could see on each call — and why did three different symptoms surface in three different offices before anyone connected them?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows the cost gap between the live options narrowing to ₹365 per bid once caching is enabled. Does that make cost irrelevant to this decision? What would have to change for it to become decisive again?
  3. Exhibit 3's footnote says the evaluation used bids the library was known to cover. How does that limitation cut — does it flatter the long-context design, the retrieval design, or both, and what additional test would you commission before 30 April?
  4. Which option should Devika take, and what precisely should Bhaashya write in answer to question 29? Distinguish between what the company can promise as a mechanism and what it can only promise as a practice.

Section 8A note for the learner

The lens for this case is the context window: the fixed span of tokens a model can condition on in a single call. Three properties of that window structure everything above. First, the window is capacity, not attention — Exhibit 3 shows that material can be inside the window and still go unused, and that where it sits matters. Second, the window has no memory: nothing persists between calls, so everything Bhaashya wants the model to know must be re-sent and re-paid for every time, which is why cost, latency and prompt length move together. Third, because the window is assembled by Bhaashya's own code, whatever enters it is a decision the company makes and can be held to — which is what turns a design choice into the answer to a security questionnaire.

A well-reasoned answer starts by naming the binding constraint. Exhibit 2 invites the reader to argue about cost, and cost is the wrong constraint here: at 3.2% of revenue in the worst case, and ₹365 per bid between the live options, no board would decide on that. The real constraints are the fourteen-point reuse regression, the twelve-minute wait that two clients are already routing around, and the fact that 53% of tokens in every request are client-attributable with no enforcement point. A strong answer also notices that the 9% superseded-answer finding is not a context-window problem at all but a data-hygiene problem the old design had been quietly solving with a validity filter — and that removing a filter is a different act from enlarging a window.

One defensible path is Option C. Selection is retained not primarily to save money but because it is the only place in the architecture where Bhaashya can enforce which client's material enters a request; that gives Devika a mechanical rather than a procedural answer to question 29, which is what a security reviewer at Al Rahba is actually asking for. Restoring retrieval as the default returns generation to ninety seconds, which addresses Lena's and Shruti's evidence directly. The long-context pass is then spent deliberately, on the small set of questions where the cost of missing a relevant past answer is losing a bid, and where a client-scoped, validity-filtered slice is small enough that caching makes the economics unremarkable. Devika would still owe Karthik something real: the two Pune engineers should not spend two quarters on retrieval, so the scope must be limited to per-client scoping and a re-ranking pass, with the ingestion backlog explicitly funded next.

Option A is defensible if — and only if — Bhaashya first moves every customer to a single-tenant index and can show a positional evaluation on novel questions rather than covered ones. Option B is defensible but spends the company's scarcest resource on rebuilding a component whose original weakness was never measured either. What is not defensible is answering question 29 with a paragraph, as Sanjay proposes, when Exhibit 4 says the paragraph would not be true.

Bhaashya Systems and Al Rahba Technology Services are fictional companies created for teaching purposes; individuals named are fictional. Infosys, TCS and Wipro appear only as market context. Figures are illustrative.

The Context Window

A fixed span of tokens, a stateless model, and an entire discipline of engineering built to disguise both. What separates a practitioner who can say the words from one who can referee the argument.

Section 1Two rooms, one constraint

On the evening of 18 February 2026, Rohit Deshmukh stayed late at Bandish Care Cloud's office in Baner, Pune, working through a spreadsheet that had begun as a routine margin review and had turned into something considerably less routine. Bandish sells an agent-assist layer to the contact centres of Indian insurers and non-banking financial companies: when a customer calls about a lapsed policy or a rejected claim, the human agent sees a suggested reply, drafted in real time, grounded in that customer's file and that product's wording. Bandish had signed twenty-two enterprise contracts, priced per conversation, and the largest of them — a health insurer running about 1.9 lakh assisted conversations a month — paid ₹14 per conversation. Rohit's spreadsheet said the current design cost ₹91.80 per conversation to serve.

Nobody had been careless. In October 2025, Bandish had upgraded from a model with a 32,000-token context window to one with 200,000, and the team had done the obvious thing: with room to spare, they stopped choosing what to send and simply sent everything — the full forty-page policy wording, the customer's three-year interaction history, the product catalogue, the compliance rules. Quality had improved. The engineering backlog had shortened by two sprints. And the cost per conversation had risen by a factor of six and a half without anyone noticing, because for four months the largest contract had still been in pilot and the volumes had been small.

Two thousand kilometres away in Hyderabad, on the same evening, Priya Venkataraman was looking at a different manifestation of the same constraint. Jharokha Health Systems runs a chronic-care app for diabetes and hypertension patients — about 6.2 lakh monthly active users, mostly in tier-one and tier-two cities, many of them referred by their treating physicians. Jharokha's newest feature generates a pre-consultation summary: before a patient walks into their endocrinologist's chamber, the doctor receives a one-page brief of the last six months. The clinical advisory board, chaired by a senior endocrinologist in Chennai, had made one demand that Priya could not argue with: the summary must not omit anything clinically material. Jharokha's median patient record ran to 312 documents across five years — prescriptions, lab reports scanned and passed through OCR, discharge summaries, the app's own logged readings — which tokenised to roughly 640,000 tokens. It fitted, barely, inside a one-million-token window. It cost ₹115 per summary against a consultation the patient paid ₹499 for. And when Priya's data scientist in Toronto, Aditi Menon, ran a blinded audit of 400 generated summaries against a clinician's own reading of the same record, the summaries missed a material item 19% of the time — despite every one of those items having been inside the window.

Rohit's problem looks like economics and Priya's looks like quality. They are the same problem seen from two sides, and the argument that runs through this page is the following: the context window is not storage and it is not memory; it is a scarce, positionally non-uniform, per-call-rebuilt resource whose allocation is a product decision, and every serious question about cost, latency, accuracy, auditability and data governance in an LLM product resolves into a question about how that allocation is made. Teams that treat the window as a container to fill get punished twice — once on the bill and once on the accuracy — and the two punishments arrive at different times, which is why the failure is so common.

Section 2The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

Define it carefully. A token is an element of a fixed vocabulary — typically a sub-word fragment — into which text is segmented before a model processes it. The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can condition on in a single forward pass, and it is shared: the prompt you send and the completion the model generates occupy the same budget. To say a model is stateless is to say that this budget is rebuilt from nothing on every call. No fact, instruction or inference survives the end of a call unless your application stores it and re-sends it.

The constraint is a consequence of an architectural choice made for reasons unrelated to it. Sequence models before 2017 — recurrent networks and long short-term memory networks in the lineage of Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's 1997 work — did maintain a genuine carried state, a fixed-size vector updated token by token. That state was in principle unbounded in reach and in practice terrible over long spans, because information had to survive many lossy updates, and it could not be computed in parallel, which capped how large such models could be trained. Bahdanau and colleagues introduced attention in 2014 as a patch: let the decoder look back at all encoder positions directly instead of relying on the compressed state. Vaswani and colleagues' 2017 paper took the patch and threw away the thing it was patching. In a transformer there is no carried state at all; every token attends to every other token in the input simultaneously. That is what made parallel training and therefore scale possible, and it is what created the window, because all-pairs attention costs compute proportional to the square of the sequence length and memory proportional to it. Someone must draw a line.

The line has moved a great deal. Early GPT-3-class models offered 2,048 tokens; by 2023 the frontier was 100,000; by 2026 million-token windows are ordinary and multi-million windows exist. The engineering that moved it is worth naming because it constrains what you can assume: rotary position embeddings and their interpolation, which let a model trained at one length operate at a longer one; attention variants that avoid computing all pairs, including sliding-window and sparse patterns; grouped-query attention, which shrinks the memory the model must hold per token; and hardware-aware implementations that keep the quadratic arithmetic from becoming the bottleneck it looks like on paper. None of these makes attention uniform across the window. Several of them explicitly make it non-uniform, and that has product consequences.

Three schools, and what each will actually sign

Practitioners of good faith disagree about what to do with this, and it is worth stating the positions in the strongest form each holds, because a PM will meet all three inside one engineering team.

The long-context school holds that selection is a lossy, hard-to-debug step that should be eliminated wherever the budget allows. Its proposition, which it will sign without hedging: given a model whose measured recall at length L is adequate for the task, sending everything relevant within L strictly dominates sending a retrieved subset, because retrieval introduces a failure mode — the right document was never fetched — that is invisible to the model and expensive to diagnose. It will not sign the stronger claim that window size makes retrieval obsolete at all volumes; its adherents concede cost readily and argue that engineering time is scarcer than tokens and that token prices fall.

The retrieval school holds that selection is not a cost-saving hack but a correctness and governance requirement. Its proposition: a system that cannot say which specific sources produced an answer cannot be audited, cannot cite, cannot enforce per-user access control, and cannot be defended to a regulator; selection is the only mechanism that produces that provenance, and its cost advantage is a side benefit. It will not sign the claim that retrieval improves raw accuracy on tasks where the whole corpus fits comfortably; several of its adherents accept that on pure accuracy, stuffing sometimes wins.

The state school — the newest and the one most visible in agent products — holds that both of the above are answers to the wrong question. Its proposition: the durable object should be an explicitly maintained, structured state (a rolling summary, an entity store, a scratchpad, a task ledger) that the system writes deliberately, and the window should hold that state plus the immediate task, because raw history and retrieved chunks both degrade as the interaction lengthens. It will not sign the claim that summarisation is lossless; it argues instead that all three options lose information and that at least this one loses it under your control and on your schedule.

Section 3Mechanics in depth, with the arithmetic

Start with the phases, because almost every operational surprise traces to confusing them. Prefill processes the entire prompt in one parallel pass and produces, for every layer and every token, a set of keys and values that later tokens will attend to. This is where time-to-first-token comes from, and it is where the quadratic term lives. Decode then emits tokens one at a time; each new token attends over the stored keys and values of every preceding token, which is why that store — the KV cache — must be held in accelerator memory for the whole life of the request.

The KV-cache arithmetic in Figure 1 is worth doing by hand once. For a model with 80 layers, 8 key-value heads under grouped-query attention, a head dimension of 128, storing keys and values in 16-bit precision, each token costs 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes, a shade over 320 KiB. A 128,000-token prompt therefore parks 40 GiB of accelerator memory for the duration of the request. An 80 GiB accelerator can hold one such request and part of another. The same accelerator serving 8,000-token prompts holds thirty of them. This is the mechanism by which long context raises unit cost even where the price per token is flat: it collapses concurrency, and concurrency is what amortises the hardware. A PM who has internalised only "long prompts cost more tokens" will mis-forecast capacity by an order of magnitude.

Prefill cost is often described as quadratic, which is true of the attention term and misleading as a summary. Total prefill work looks like a linear term (the feed-forward layers, proportional to n) plus a quadratic term (attention, proportional to n²). At short lengths the linear term dominates and doubling the prompt roughly doubles the time; somewhere in the tens of thousands of tokens the quadratic term takes over and the curve bends. Bandish measured its own, on its own hardware, and the shape is Exhibit 1.

Read the last column rather than the second. Four times the tokens costs 4.2, then 4.6, then 5.0 times the time: the curve is bending, slowly, exactly as the two-term model predicts. For Bandish this was decisive in a way cost was not, because the product sits beside a live human agent on a telephone call. Seventeen seconds of silence while an assist suggestion loads is not a degraded experience; it is an unusable one. The agents in the insurer's Noida centre had, Bandish's customer-success lead in Singapore reported, simply stopped waiting for the suggestion and started typing their own replies — a quality failure that would never have shown up in an accuracy metric.

Then there is the step almost every team leaves implicit: serialisation. The model does not receive your documents as documents. Your application concatenates everything into one flat sequence with role markers and delimiters, and every choice in that concatenation — order, headers, whether you include filenames, whether you inject a timestamp — is a design decision with measurable effect. Two teams sending "the same" material can get materially different accuracy. It is also where prompt caching lives or dies: caching matches on an exact prefix, so a variable element placed early (a session ID, the current time, a re-sorted document list) invalidates everything after it. Bandish discovered a 3.1× cost regression that traced to a well-intentioned change putting the conversation's start time at the top of the system prompt.

Section 4When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

The useful form of "it depends" is a set of claims you can test on your own product this week. Four of them do most of the work.

Claim one: if calls per month × tokens per call × price per token is a material fraction of revenue from those calls, selection is mandatory rather than optional. For Bandish, 1.9 lakh conversations × 6.4 turns × 68,300 tokens is 8.3 billion input tokens a month; at ₹210 per million that is ₹1.74 crore against contract revenue of ₹26.6 lakh. The claim tests true, emphatically. For Jharokha the arithmetic is subtler: 640,000 tokens at ₹180 per million is ₹115 against a ₹499 consultation, and summaries are generated once per consultation rather than per turn — 23% of revenue, painful but survivable, so the claim tests true but not decisively.

Claim two: if time-to-first-token above two seconds degrades the experience, prompt length is a latency budget before it is a cost budget. True for Bandish, where a human is on a live call; false for Jharokha, where the summary is generated overnight before a scheduled appointment and a ninety-second batch job is invisible. This is why the same fact pattern produces opposite designs, and why a PM who has memorised "long context is expensive" without the latency dimension will give Priya the wrong advice.

Claim three: if the task requires combining facts that are far apart in the prompt, effective context is much shorter than advertised context. Retrieving one stated fact from a long document is easy for modern models. Noticing that a lab value in document 41 contradicts a medication in document 297 and that the combination matters is a different task, and it degrades much faster with length. Jharokha's 19% miss rate is almost entirely of this second kind: Aditi's error analysis in Toronto found that 71% of misses involved two documents more than 200,000 tokens apart in the serialised record.

Claim four: if any part of the window is subject to per-user access control, residency or retention rules, selection is a compliance mechanism and cannot be replaced by a larger window. Both companies test true here. Bandish's insurer customers operate under IRDAI supervision and expect to see exactly which policy clauses informed a statement made to a customer. Jharokha handles health data under the DPDP Act, where purpose limitation and the patient's right to erasure both imply that "we send the entire record every time" is a position the company would have to defend rather than assume.

There is also a situation where the idea is actively misleading, and it deserves to be said plainly. For a genuinely small corpus — a 30-page product manual, a policy document, a single contract — building a retrieval layer is over-engineering that adds a failure mode nobody needed. The team spends six weeks on chunking strategy to save ₹4,000 a month and introduces the possibility that the right chunk is never fetched. "Always retrieve" is as thoughtless a rule as "always stuff". The discriminating question is not which is better but where the crossover sits for your volumes, your latency budget and your governance obligations.

Section 5Hard edge cases

Two-sided and marketplace products. When one model serves both sides of a market, the window becomes an authorisation surface. A commerce platform's assistant that helps a seller price a listing must see competitor price bands in aggregate but not identified buyer histories; the buyer-facing assistant must see the reverse. The naive design — one big prompt with everything, and an instruction telling the model not to reveal certain parts — is not access control, because an instruction is a request, not a mechanism. Mature teams enforce this before assembly: the retrieval layer is scoped by the caller's identity, so material the caller may not see never enters the window at all. This is a strong argument for the retrieval school that has nothing to do with cost.

Regulated products. In financial services under RBI or SEBI supervision, and in insurance under IRDAI, the operative question during an audit is not "was the model accurate" but "can you reconstruct what the system considered when it made this statement, on this date". Statelessness is unexpectedly helpful here: because every call is self-contained, logging the exact serialised prompt gives you perfect reproducibility. Teams that log only the user's message and the model's reply have thrown away the evidence. Bandish's compliance lead insisted on storing prompt hashes and the retrieval decision trace for seven years, which turned out to cost more in storage than the team had budgeted and to be the single most valuable thing they did.

Hardware and on-device. Where a model runs on a phone or an embedded device, the window is bounded by memory rather than by policy, and the KV-cache arithmetic above becomes the whole story. A 4,000-token practical window on a mid-range Android handset is a different product than a million-token cloud window, and the interesting designs are hybrid: a small on-device model handles the immediate turn while a cloud model handles the long-context work, with the split invisible to the user and highly visible in the failure modes.

AI-native and agentic products. This is where the window behaves least like a container. An agent that calls tools reads their outputs back into the same window; a single web fetch or a verbose API response can consume 20,000 tokens, and after fifteen tool calls the window is dominated by material the agent no longer needs. Practitioners call the resulting degradation context rot. The mature response is not a bigger window but explicit context management: summarising or discarding tool outputs after use, keeping a compact task ledger, and re-injecting the objective near the end of the prompt so it is not buried under transcripts.

The organisational seam. The most consistent failure in large companies is that nobody owns the window. The platform team owns the model gateway, the feature teams own the prompts, and the finance team owns the bill. Prompts grow because every team adds a paragraph to fix its own edge case and nobody removes anything, and the total is not anyone's metric. What mature companies actually do, as opposed to what their architecture diagrams say, is impose a token budget per feature at the gateway, publish tokens-per-call by feature weekly, and require a review when a prompt template grows by more than a set percentage. It is mundane, and it is the difference between a 40% annual inference cost increase and a 300% one.

Section 6The nuances that separate expert from competent

1. Distractors are worse than absence

The competent practitioner believes that adding a document can only help or be neutral. The expert knows that adding plausible-but-irrelevant material measurably degrades accuracy, sometimes below the level achieved with no supporting documents at all, because the model must now discriminate rather than merely read. The tell in the wild: accuracy improves when the team removes a source. The obvious reading — "that source was wrong" — is usually incorrect; the source was right and merely similar enough to the answer to compete for attention.

2. Advertised context is a ceiling, effective context is an empirical result

The tell is a team quoting the vendor's number in a design document. Experts quote their own number, measured on their own task at their own length, and quote two of them: one for lookup and one for multi-hop reasoning. The gap between those two is often 4:1, and it is the single most useful number a team can put on the wall.

3. Needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks are necessary and badly insufficient

Planting a distinctive sentence in a long document and asking for it back is easy for modern models precisely because the sentence is distinctive — it stands out from its surroundings the way a red tile stands out on a white floor. Real tasks require finding material that resembles everything around it. The expert's tell: they build the needle out of the same vocabulary as the haystack, and their measured recall drops by twenty points when they do.

4. Caching is a property of the prefix, not of the content

Everyone learns that caching saves money. The expert has internalised that it saves money only for a byte-identical leading segment reused within a short window, and therefore designs the prompt in stability order: immutable system content first, slowly-changing customer content next, per-call content last. The tell is a template whose variable fields are all at the bottom. The obvious alternative — putting the customer's name at the top, which reads better — quietly costs a multiple of the bill.

5. Long context changes the shape of errors, not just their rate

With a short window a model that lacks a fact says it does not know. With a long window containing a superseded 2023 version of the same policy, it answers confidently from the wrong document. The expert recognises that moving to long context converts abstentions into confident errors, which is a worse failure class in regulated products, and responds by adding recency and authority metadata to every document in the window rather than by trusting the model to sort it out.

6. The window is a shared budget with the output and the tools

The tell is a team that has never written down its allocation. Experts maintain a context budget: so many tokens for system and tools, so many for retrieved material, so many for history, and an explicit reserve for the completion. Reserving output headroom is not optional; a prompt filled to 99% of the window produces a truncated answer, and truncated answers in a structured-output pipeline produce malformed JSON, which produces an outage rather than a quality dip.

7. Tokenisation is not language-neutral, and in India that is a first-order effect

Jharokha's Telugu and Bengali content consumed 2.4 and 2.1 times the tokens per unit of meaning as its English content, because sub-word vocabularies are dominated by English training data and Indic scripts fragment heavily. A 200,000-token window is a 90,000-token window in Telugu. The tell is a team whose cost model has one tokens-per-page constant. Experts hold a distribution by language and document type, and they price multilingual expansion accordingly rather than discovering it in the quarterly review.

8. Position is a lever you own, and it is nearly free

Because attention is non-uniform, where you place material is a design parameter. Putting the decisive material immediately adjacent to the question, and repeating critical constraints near the end of the prompt, routinely buys several points of accuracy for zero incremental cost. The tell: a team whose prompt has an explicit, documented ordering rationale. The competent practitioner treats prompt order as arbitrary; the expert treats it as configuration to be tested.

9. Statelessness is a debugging asset

Because nothing carries over, any call can be replayed exactly if you logged the serialised prompt. Teams that log the user's message alone are unable to reproduce their own bugs and end up arguing from anecdote. The tell in the wild: an incident review in which someone can paste the exact 68,000-token prompt that produced the bad answer, and the room goes quiet because the cause is immediately visible.

10. Memory is a product feature you build, with its own lifecycle

Users say "the assistant remembers me". No model does. Your system stores, selects and re-injects. That means memory has retention rules, deletion obligations under the DPDP Act, a decay policy, a correction mechanism when what it remembered is wrong, and a per-call token cost that grows with tenure. The tell: a team that can answer "what happens to the memory when a user asks us to forget them" without a meeting.

Section 7How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products, volume dominates and per-user willingness to pay is low, so the context budget is tight and aggressive summarisation is normal. The compensating advantage is that consumer users tolerate mild forgetting; the cost of a miss is irritation. In B2B and enterprise, the cost of a miss is contractual, buyers ask what data enters the prompt during security review, and per-seat pricing means a single heavy user can be gross-margin negative on their own — so enterprise teams need per-account token telemetry, which consumer teams rarely bother with. In platform and marketplace products the differentiating issue is scoping by participant, discussed above. For hardware and physical goods, honesty requires saying that outside on-device inference the difference is small: a connected appliance calling a cloud model faces the same economics as any other client, and the interesting constraint is intermittent connectivity rather than window size. For AI-native products the window is the central design object rather than a parameter, and context engineering is a named discipline with owners.

Stage changes the correct answer more than product type does. At seed stage with a few hundred calls a day, stuff the window: engineering time is the binding constraint, the bill is noise, and a retrieval layer built before you know the query distribution is a layer built on guesses. The single discipline required is instrumentation, so that the crossover is visible when it arrives. At growth stage, inference becomes a real line in cost of goods sold and someone must own the budget. At enterprise scale the question changes again, from cost to governance: which material is permitted in which window, provable to an auditor. Bandish at ₹31 crore of ARR and Jharokha at 6.2 lakh users were both at the growth-stage crossover, which is why both discovered the problem in the same quarter.

Example B — Jharokha, where cost is not the binding constraint

Priya's summaries cost ₹115 each against ₹499 of revenue, which is survivable. Her problem is the 19% material-miss rate, and the instinct in the room — offered by two engineers in Bengaluru — was to move to a model with a larger window so that the OCR'd lab scans could be included at full fidelity rather than truncated. Aditi's error analysis in Toronto killed the idea with one table: of 76 misses in the 400-summary audit, 54 involved facts that were both present in the prompt and separated by more than 200,000 tokens, 14 involved a superseded prescription being preferred over a current one, and only 8 involved material that had been truncated out. A larger window addresses eight of seventy-six. Restructuring the record into a chronologically ordered, deduplicated clinical timeline with explicit recency markers — 34,000 tokens instead of 640,000 — addressed the other sixty-eight and cut the cost to ₹6.10.

Example C — the failure, and what recovery actually looked like

Bandish's October 2025 migration is the cautionary one. The team moved to the 200,000-token model, appended the product catalogue to the existing prompt, and shipped. Customer satisfaction rose 3.1 points in the first fortnight, which everyone read as validation. In week five, the insurer's quality team flagged four calls in which the assist had suggested a premium figure that was not the customer's current premium. Nobody had changed the compliance instruction that forbade quoting premium amounts; it was still in the prompt. It had simply moved. Appending 12,000 tokens of catalogue had pushed that instruction from roughly 15% of the way through the prompt to roughly 58%, into the region of weakest attention, and adherence fell from 99.4% to 94.7% — a rate that looks fine on a dashboard and is unacceptable when the absolute number is nine hundred conversations a month.

The recovery took eleven weeks and had three parts, none of them a model change. First, hard constraints were pinned at both the start and the end of the prompt, which restored adherence to 99.1%. Second, a deterministic post-check was added outside the model: a regular-expression pass that blocked any suggestion containing a currency figure not present in the retrieved customer record. Third — and this is the part that mattered organisationally — Bandish added a rule that any change to the prompt template of more than 2,000 tokens required a re-run of the adherence suite before release. The lesson Rohit drew was not "long context is bad" but "prompt structure is a release artefact and must be treated like code".

Section 9Failure modes, warnings and diagnostics

Silent truncation. Early warning: quality degrades as sessions get longer, and support tickets cluster on power users. Diagnostic question: what is our truncation policy, who wrote it, and how many calls hit it last week? Cost of catching late: months of unexplained quality complaints and, in the worst version, a system instruction dropped without any error.

Prompt creep. Early warning: mean tokens per call rising a few percent a week with no feature launch. Diagnostic: plot tokens per call by feature over ninety days. Cost of catching late: a bill that has tripled and a prompt nobody dares to prune because they no longer know which paragraph fixes which bug.

Cache invalidation. Early warning: cost and latency both rise on a day with no model change and no traffic change. Diagnostic: is cache hit rate an instrumented metric, and did it drop? Cost of catching late: Bandish's 3.1× regression, which ran for nineteen days.

Distractor poisoning. Early warning: accuracy falls after a release that added a data source. Diagnostic: ablate — remove one source at a time and re-run the eval. Cost of catching late: a permanent accuracy ceiling that the team attributes to the model and tries to fix by upgrading it.

Concurrency collapse. Early warning: latency degrades sharply at peak — for Indian consumer products, the Diwali or festival-sale evening — while average utilisation looks moderate. Diagnostic: compute KV-cache bytes per request at the ninety-fifth-percentile prompt length and divide into accelerator memory. Cost of catching late: an outage on the highest-revenue day of the year.

Evaluating on prompts shorter than production. Early warning: the eval suite passes at 99% and production accuracy is visibly worse. Diagnostic: compare the length distribution of eval prompts against the length distribution of real ones. Cost of catching late: an entire quarter of confident, wrong decisions built on a measurement that never tested the failure mode.

Section 10Where experts genuinely disagree

Does retrieval remain necessary as windows grow? The long-context position, steelmanned: retrieval failures are the dominant source of production errors in deployed systems, they are silent, and the engineering to make retrieval good — chunking, hybrid search, re-ranking, freshness — is a permanent tax on a small team. Token prices have fallen roughly an order of magnitude every eighteen months, so a cost objection is a temporary objection. This would be wrong if positional degradation on multi-hop tasks turns out to be structural rather than a training artefact, or if provenance obligations become binding in a way that a stuffed window cannot satisfy. The retrieval position, steelmanned: cost and latency are real today and users experience latency immediately; provenance and per-caller scoping cannot be delegated to an instruction; and the corpora that matter in enterprise settings are terabytes, so the window will never hold them regardless of growth. This would be wrong if models reached uniform attention across multi-million-token windows at a price competitive with retrieval, and if scoping could be enforced some other way.

Is "lost in the middle" durable? One camp treats it as an artefact of training-data length distributions that later models will fix, and points to newer models whose needle tests are near-flat. The other treats it as structural: attention weight is a normalised, finite resource, so as sequence length grows the weight available to any single token falls, and no amount of training removes that. The honest current state is that flat needle curves coexist with steep multi-hop curves, which is consistent with both stories. What would settle it is a public benchmark of same-vocabulary, multi-hop retrieval at length, run across model generations — which does not yet exist in a form the field agrees on.

Should memory be summarised or retrieved? The summarisation camp argues that a maintained rolling state is compact, cheap and stable, and that users care about the gist rather than the transcript. The retrieval camp argues that summarisation discards exactly the specific detail — a date, an account number, an earlier promise — that users notice when it is lost, and that a summary's errors compound because each summary is generated from the last. Both are right about the other's weakness. Most sophisticated products now run both, with a summary for continuity and retrieval over the verbatim transcript for specifics, and the disagreement has moved to how to decide which one answers a given question.

Section 11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can define a token and quote a window size. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. They ask "what is actually in the window on this call" as their first diagnostic question for any quality complaint, before asking about the model or the prompt wording, and they expect to be shown the serialised prompt rather than a description of it. They hold a context budget with an owner and a review cadence, and they treat a prompt-template change like a code change, with an eval gate. They quote two effective-context numbers for their own task rather than one advertised number for the model. And they can say, without preparation, what a call costs, what it costs at ten times the volume, and which segment of the prompt they would cut first — which means they have already decided what the product can afford to forget.

Section 12Closing: two decisions

Rohit's decision, taken on 24 February, was to keep the long-context design for the highest-value 6% of conversations — claim disputes above ₹2 lakh, where a miss is expensive and volume is low — and to move everything else to a retrieval-plus-rolling-summary design with hard constraints pinned at both ends of the prompt. He also renegotiated the metric in the insurer's contract from cost per conversation to cost per conversation at a stated latency, because his real constraint had always been the two-second budget rather than the ₹14 one, and pretending otherwise had produced four months of the wrong optimisation.

Priya's decision was to stop treating the record as a corpus and start treating it as a maintained state. Jharokha would build a clinical timeline — deduplicated, chronologically ordered, with explicit supersession markers so a discontinued medication is labelled as discontinued rather than merely older — updated incrementally as new documents arrive, and send that timeline plus the retrieved originals for anything the timeline flagged as uncertain. She accepted, and told her advisory board explicitly, that this design can lose information the raw record contains, and that the question is not whether to lose information but whether to lose it deliberately at build time or accidentally at inference time.

Three questions in the style of a teaching note.

1. Rohit's contract prices per conversation while his binding constraint is latency per turn. What would have had to be true at the time of signing for per-conversation pricing to have been the right structure, and what should Bandish's pricing look like across its other twenty-one contracts?

2. Priya's clinical timeline is a lossy compression chosen by her team. If a material item is missed because the timeline dropped it, is the failure different in kind from one where the item sat unattended in the middle of a 640,000-token prompt? Who is accountable in each case, and does the answer change under the DPDP Act?

3. Suppose the price per token falls by 90% over the next eighteen months and effective context becomes flat to a million tokens. Which of the two companies' decisions should be reversed, and which should stand on grounds that have nothing to do with cost?

Section 13Going deeper

  1. Tokens and tokenisation — the unit the window is measured in; without it, every cost and capacity estimate on this page is guesswork, and the Indic-language multipliers are invisible.
  2. What a large language model actually is — establishes that prediction conditions only on the window, which is the reason statelessness is a property of the model rather than a limitation of an API.
  3. The transformer and attention — explains why the window exists at all, why cost grows faster than linearly, and why attention is non-uniform across position; it turns Figure 1 from a fact into a prediction.
  4. Vector search and similarity — the mechanism by which a retrieval layer decides which twelve clauses or three lab reports to send, and where its silent failures come from.
  5. System prompts and message roles — the structure imposed on the flat token sequence, and the reason instruction placement is a lever rather than an aesthetic choice.
  6. Latency, throughput and the cost of a token — converts Exhibit 1 and the KV-cache arithmetic into a capacity model you can plan a festival peak against.
  7. Prompt caching — the single highest-leverage cost intervention available without changing product behaviour, and the one most easily destroyed by an innocuous template edit.
  8. Retrieval-augmented generation as an architecture — the full form of the "select then send" design, including the failure modes that make the long-context school suspicious of it.
  9. Agents and tool use — where the window stops being filled once and becomes consumed turn by turn, and where context rot becomes the dominant failure mode.
  10. Embeddings — the representation that makes similarity computable, and therefore makes selection possible at scale.
  11. Inference versus training — clarifies that nothing you put in the window changes the model, which is the confusion behind half the questions executives ask about "teaching it our data".
  12. Pre-training, post-training and fine-tuning — the alternative to putting knowledge in the window: moving it into the weights, with a completely different cost and update profile.
  13. RLHF and alignment — why models follow instructions in the window at all, and why adherence is statistical rather than guaranteed.
  14. LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning — the practical middle path for the stable, high-volume portion of a prompt that never changes.
  15. Quantisation — reduces the bytes per parameter and per cached token, directly relaxing the concurrency constraint that Figure 1 makes visible.

The Context Window

If the window is huge now, can you simply put everything in it and stop worrying? Adhyaay Legal Cloud spent one quarter finding out.

Section 1An expensive Tuesday in Bengaluru

On Tuesday, 10 March 2026, Meera Rajagopalan, vice-president of product at Adhyaay Legal Cloud, sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of an office block off Bannerghatta Road with two numbers on the whiteboard behind her. The first was ₹9.8 crore. The second was 4.6. Adhyaay sells a contract-review assistant to in-house legal teams — thirty-eight enterprise customers, most of them Indian manufacturing and financial-services groups, plus a growing set of GCCs in Hyderabad and Pune. A lawyer uploads a counterparty's redlined agreement; the product returns a memo saying which changes are acceptable under the company's own negotiation playbook, which are not, and what to counter-propose.

The engineering lead, Faisal Qureshi, had proposed something that sounded like simplification. The model Adhyaay used had just moved to a one-million-token context window. Why, he asked, keep maintaining the retrieval layer — the clause index, the embedding pipeline, the chunking rules, the two engineers who nursed it — when the entire contract estate for a single customer could now be pasted into a single call? Delete the machinery. Ship faster. His slide had four words on it: put it all in.

Meera's hesitation was not sentimental. The ₹9.8 crore was what Adhyaay's inference bill would become in a year if the roadmap's clause-monitoring feature launched with Faisal's design at the volumes sales had already sold. The 4.6 was the ratio her own team had measured between the cost of stuffing everything into the window and the cost of selecting what mattered. But the harder problem was not cost. Three weeks earlier, a customer in Coimbatore had found that the assistant missed an uncapped confidentiality indemnity that sat on page 27 of a 42-page master services agreement — an agreement that had been fully inside the window at the time. The model had been shown the clause and had not used it. Meera needed to explain, by Friday, why a bigger window had not fixed that, and what she intended to do instead.

Section 2The idea, stated precisely

A context window is the fixed maximum span of tokens that a language model can condition on within one call. A token is the unit into which text is chopped before the model sees it — roughly three-quarters of an English word, so 1,000 tokens is about 750 words of ordinary prose. To condition on something means the model's prediction of the next token is computed as a function of it. Anything inside the window can influence the output. Anything outside it cannot, in the same way that a fact you did not tell someone cannot influence their answer, however true it is.

The second half of the definition matters more than the first, and it is the half people skip. The window is not memory. A language model, as deployed in almost every product a PM will build on, is stateless: it retains nothing between calls. When your product sends a second message in what the user experiences as a continuous conversation, the model is not remembering the first message — your application is re-sending it. The illusion of memory is an engineering achievement of your own system, not a property of the model. The window is a whiteboard that is photographed, acted upon, and then wiped completely clean; whatever you want on it next time, you must write again, and you must pay to write it again.

This constraint has a history worth thirty seconds. The architectures that preceded the transformer — recurrent networks, and then long short-term memory networks from the 1990s — genuinely did carry a compressed hidden state forward through a sequence, which is a kind of memory, but they degraded badly over long spans and could not be trained in parallel. The transformer architecture, published by Vaswani and colleagues at Google in 2017, threw the recurrence away and replaced it with attention: every token is compared against every other token in the input, all at once. That is what made training fast enough to produce today's models. It also created the window, because comparing every token with every other token means the cost of a call grows roughly with the square of the input length, so somebody has to draw a line and say: no more than this many.

The sentence Meera could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "The context window is everything the model can see in one call, measured in tokens, and it is the only thing it can see — nothing carries over unless we put it back in ourselves, and putting more in costs more without guaranteeing the model uses it."

Section 3How it actually works, step by step

Walk the mechanics through Adhyaay's product. A lawyer at a customer in Coimbatore uploads a redline. Adhyaay's backend assembles a request. First a system prompt — standing instructions about tone, format and what the assistant must never do. Then tool definitions, the machine-readable descriptions of functions the model may call, which occupy tokens whether or not any tool is used. Then whatever documents the product decided to include. Then the conversation so far, which the backend has been storing in its own database. Then the lawyer's new question.

All of that is flattened into a single sequence and passed through the tokeniser, which converts characters into integers from a fixed vocabulary. The count of those integers is what is measured against the window. The model then runs its prefill pass: it processes the whole input at once and builds an internal representation of it, which is why long prompts are slow to start answering even when the answer itself is short. Only then does it begin decoding — emitting output tokens one at a time, each new token appended to the sequence and conditioned on everything before it. That is the step practitioners leave implicit: the output is written into the same window as the input. A 200,000-token window holding a 199,000-token prompt has room for a thousand tokens of answer and no more.

When the reply is finished, the call ends and the state is discarded. If the lawyer asks a follow-up, Adhyaay's backend loads the stored transcript, decides how much of it to include, re-assembles the whole request, and pays for all of it again. Two engineering conveniences complicate this picture in useful ways. Prompt caching lets a provider keep the processed representation of a stable prefix for a short time, so the identical opening of a request need not be recomputed — cheaper and faster, but only if the prefix is byte-identical and reused inside the cache's lifetime. And a truncation policy — the rule your system applies when the assembled request exceeds the window — must exist whether or not anyone designed it. Adhyaay's, discovered rather than chosen, silently dropped the oldest messages.

At 260,000 calls a month the annual bill falls from ₹9.85 crore to ₹2.13 crore, a saving of ₹7.7 crore. Caching complicates this honestly rather than reversing it. Suppose 84,000 of the stuffed request's tokens are stable across a review session and the provider bills cached reads at 10% of the input rate, with a 25% premium on the first write. Call one costs ₹34.43; calls two to five cost ₹10.28 each; the five-call average is ₹15.11. Caching roughly halves the stuffed design's cost — and it is real money — but the selected design remains less than half of that again, and the cached prefix must be byte-identical, which means a single re-ordered document or a timestamp injected at the top destroys the saving without any error message to tell you so.

Section 5The nuances a learner must acquire

A window is capacity, not attention

This is the nuance that explains Meera's Coimbatore incident. Fitting inside the window guarantees only that the model could use a fact; it says nothing about whether it did. Attention distributes finite weight across everything present, and empirically that weight is not uniform. Adhyaay's team ran the standard diagnostic: they planted one decisive sentence — an uncapped confidentiality indemnity — at ten positions in a 120,000-token prompt and asked 200 questions at each position. Recall was 96% when the sentence sat in the first tenth of the prompt, 92% in the last tenth, and 71% in the middle. This "lost in the middle" pattern, first characterised systematically in 2023, is why page 27 of 42 was the most dangerous place in the document for that clause to live.

Input and output share one budget

Product managers routinely specify "a 4,000-word report" against a prompt they have already filled to the brim, then are baffled when the output stops mid-sentence. The window is the total. Reserve output headroom explicitly, and know that most providers also cap output separately at a figure far below the window — a million-token window with a 64,000-token output cap is a common shape, and the smaller number is usually the one that bites.

Advertised window and effective window are different quantities

A vendor's stated window is the length at which the model will not return an error. The length at which it still performs the task reliably is an empirical question, usually smaller, and task-dependent: simple fact-lookup holds up far longer than multi-step reasoning that must combine three facts scattered across the input. Treat the advertised number as a hard ceiling and your own measured number as the design limit.

Tokens are not words, and are not language-neutral

Adhyaay's Hindi and Tamil pilots consumed two to three times the tokens per unit of meaning as English, because tokenisers are trained predominantly on English text and split Devanagari and Tamil script into many more pieces. A window of 200,000 tokens is meaningfully smaller when the contracts are in Hindi, and the per-review cost rises with it. Any Indian product with multilingual ambitions should price and size its window per language, not on an English average.

Cost and latency rise with what you send, not with what you need

Every token in the prompt is paid for and processed even if it turns out to be irrelevant. This is the sense in which "just put it all in" is a decision to buy insurance at full price on every transaction. It is a legitimate purchase when the failure cost is high and the volume is low — and an indefensible one when the volume is 260,000 calls a month.

Recency and ordering are levers you control

Because position affects attention, where you place a document is a design choice with measurable consequences. Putting the actual question last and the decisive material either first or immediately adjacent to the question is a cheap intervention that Adhyaay's team found worth several points of accuracy — cheaper than any model change and available on day one.

The window is not the same as your product's memory

Users experience "the assistant remembers my company's style" as memory. It is a retrieval-and-re-injection system your team built. That distinction determines who owns the bug when memory fails, what your DPDP Act obligations are for the stored transcript, and whether a customer can ask you to delete what the product knows about them. A model cannot forget something it never stored; your database can, and must.

What the window cannot tell you

Knowing the window size tells you nothing about whether the material you put in it is correct, current, or complete. It is a plumbing constraint, not an epistemic one. A model given a superseded 2023 version of a policy inside a perfectly-sized window will answer confidently and wrongly. The thoughtful newcomer should therefore ask, before relying on any of this: what exactly is going into the window on each call, who decides, what gets dropped when it overflows, how do we know the model used the part that mattered, and what does this cost per call at ten times today's volume?

Section 6How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the binding constraint is usually latency and unit economics rather than accuracy. A consumer chat assistant serving lakhs of free users cannot afford a 100,000-token prompt per turn; the design question becomes how aggressively to summarise conversation history, and the acceptable answer is often quite aggressive, because a user who has to re-state something is mildly annoyed rather than materially harmed. In B2B products like Adhyaay's, the calculus inverts: a single missed indemnity can cost a customer more than a year of subscription, so teams will spend tokens to reduce miss rates — but they will also be asked, during procurement, exactly what data leaves the customer's tenancy and enters a prompt, which turns window contents into a contractual matter.

Marketplace and platform products face a third problem, which is that the context differs per participant. A seller-side assistant on a commerce platform needs the seller's catalogue, pricing rules and recent disputes; the buyer-side assistant needs order history and delivery status; and the platform's trust-and-safety assistant needs both but is legally constrained in what it may show either side. The window becomes an access-control surface: the question is not only "what helps the model" but "what is this party entitled to have the model see".

Stage changes the answer more than most PMs expect. At an early-stage company with 200 calls a day, stuffing the window is correct: engineering time is the scarce resource, the bill is noise, and the retrieval layer you would build now is a layer you would rebuild anyway once you knew what users asked. The discipline is to instrument token usage from day one so the crossover is visible. At scale, inference becomes a cost of goods sold that shows up in gross margin, and a company with 260,000 calls a month has a finance director who will notice. Adhyaay was, uncomfortably, at exactly the crossover.

Section 7Common mistakes and the cheapest way to catch them

Mistake one: treating the model as if it remembers. The symptom, observed from the outside, is a product that behaves brilliantly in a short demo and forgets a crucial instruction forty turns into a real session. The underlying misunderstanding is that the conversation lives inside the model. The cheapest diagnostic is to log the exact serialised prompt for the failing turn and read it: nine times in ten the instruction simply is not there, because a truncation rule nobody designed dropped the oldest messages first — and the oldest message is usually the system-level instruction the user gave at the start.

Mistake two: assuming inclusion equals use. The symptom is a confident answer that contradicts a document the team knows was in the prompt. The misunderstanding is conflating capacity with attention. The diagnostic is the needle test Adhyaay ran, and it takes an afternoon: plant a decisive, unambiguous fact at several positions in a prompt of realistic length, ask a question only that fact can answer, and plot accuracy against position.

Mistake three: budgeting the window in words or pages. The symptom is intermittent truncation errors that correlate with nothing obvious — until someone notices they cluster on Tamil-language documents or on contracts with heavy tabular schedules. The misunderstanding is that tokens track words. The diagnostic is to run the tokeniser over a representative sample of real customer content, by language and document type, and record the actual tokens-per-page distribution rather than the mean.

Mistake four: pricing a feature before measuring its prompt. The symptom is a feature that is enthusiastically sold and then quietly gross-margin negative. The misunderstanding is that inference cost is a rounding error, which was true at pilot volumes. The diagnostic is a one-line calculation done before the pricing meeting rather than after: tokens per call × calls per account per month × rate, compared against the monthly price of the account.

Section 8What good looks like

A team handling this well does four unglamorous things. It maintains an explicit context budget — a written allocation of the window across system prompt, retrieved material, history and reserved output, reviewed like any other budget, with a named owner. It has a deliberate truncation and summarisation policy, so that when the budget is exceeded the system drops the least valuable material rather than the oldest. It runs a positional recall test against its own content whenever the model version or the prompt structure changes, and treats a drop in mid-prompt recall as a release blocker. And it reports tokens per call alongside latency and error rate on the same dashboard, so that a prompt that quietly grew by 40% after a template change is visible within a day rather than at the next quarterly review.

Section 9What Meera decided

On Friday, 13 March, Meera did not choose between Faisal's proposal and the status quo. She split the product by failure cost. For the low-volume, high-stakes path — a lawyer actively reviewing a redline, a few thousand calls a month — Adhyaay would stuff the window generously, because ₹31 per review against a decision worth lakhs is obviously worth paying, and because the extra material demonstrably reduced misses on unusual clause structures. For the high-volume clause-monitoring path, retrieval stayed, and the two engineers stayed with it. In both paths she required the decisive material to be placed adjacent to the question rather than buried mid-prompt, and she added tokens-per-call to the weekly operating review. The reasoning she gave the board was one sentence: the window is a budget you spend, and the right amount to spend depends entirely on what a miss costs.

What to learn next follows directly from the mechanics above. The transformer and attention explains why position affects recall and why cost grows faster than linearly, turning the lost-in-the-middle curve from a mysterious empirical fact into a predictable one. Vector search and similarity and retrieval-augmented generation are the machinery behind Exhibit 2 — how a system decides which twelve clauses to send. Prompt caching and latency, throughput and the cost of a token turn the arithmetic above into an operating discipline. And agents and tool use is where the window stops being a container you fill once and becomes a resource consumed turn by turn as a model calls tools and reads their outputs back into the same finite space.

Two questions to sit with.

First: for a product you know, what exactly is in the window on a typical call — every segment, with a token count — and who on the team could answer that today without looking it up?

Second: if your model's window doubled tomorrow at the same price per token, which decision in your product would you actually change, and which would you not? The second list is usually longer than people expect, and knowing why is the difference between using the vocabulary and understanding the idea.
