Aavartan Systems: The Long Conversation

Eleven days of duplicate refunds, two cost models that disagree by thirty-nine per cent, a festival peak in thirteen days, and a board meeting at nine in the morning.

Section 1Bengaluru, Sunday night, 4 October 2026

Ira Bhattacharya had been at her kitchen table since eight, and the rain on the Sarjapur Road side of the building had not let up. On the laptop were three documents she could not reconcile: a finance model that said Aavartan Systems was losing ₹3.40 on every conversation it served, an engineering model that said it was making ₹5.40, and an incident report about ₹18.4 lakh of duplicate refunds that had gone out over eleven days in September without anyone noticing. The board met at nine on Monday. Renu had asked for fifteen minutes on "AI unit economics". Naresh had asked for zero minutes on anything, on the grounds that the festival peak began on the seventeenth and the last thing a company needed thirteen days before its highest-volume fortnight was a strategy discussion.

Ira was Chief Product Officer. She had joined Aavartan in early 2024 from a payments company, and she had spent the last fortnight learning, in an unhurried and humiliating sequence, that she did not know what her product actually sent to the model on any given message.

Section 2Company history, and the decision that still binds

Aavartan Systems was founded in Pune in 2022 and moved its commercial headquarters to Bengaluru two years later. Its product, Bolchaal, is an autonomous customer-support agent that runs on the WhatsApp Business Platform for Indian direct-to-consumer and quick-commerce brands. A customer messages a brand about a missing order, a return, a size exchange or a refund; Bolchaal reads the message, looks up the order, checks the courier status, applies the brand's policy and — this was the part that won deals — actually completes the action, initiating the refund through the brand's payment gateway rather than raising a ticket for a human.

Forty-one brands used it, from a large personal-care company to three quick-commerce operators, at a blended ₹28 per resolved conversation against roughly ₹31 for a human agent in a tier-two contact centre. Annual recurring revenue stood at ₹31 crore. Volume ran at about 9 lakh conversations a month, rising to a forecast 21 lakh in the festival month.

The decision that constrains everything is from March 2024. To win a large enterprise account, Aavartan committed in writing that no customer conversation data would leave Indian territory, and it architected accordingly: all inference runs against its model provider's Mumbai region. That commitment is now in nineteen contracts. The Mumbai region offers a 200,000-token context window. The provider's global endpoints offer a one-million-token window and two newer model families; Mumbai's roadmap for those is described by the provider's account team as "planned, not committed". In the same negotiation, Aavartan traded volume for price: a three-year agreement running to January 2027 with a minimum monthly spend of ₹1.1 crore in exchange for a rate roughly 40% below list. Everything about Bolchaal's design — how much it sends, what it can promise a client, what it costs — is downstream of those two clauses.

Section 3The industry around it

Indian D2C support automation is crowded and price-transparent. Brands compare Bolchaal against building in-house on an off-the-shelf model, against conversational-AI platforms from established Indian software firms such as Freshworks and Zoho, and against simply hiring more agents in Indore or Coimbatore. Quick-commerce players like Zepto and Swiggy Instamart have set consumer expectations for resolution inside a single chat, which is why "hand off to a human" is a harder sell than it was two years ago. WhatsApp's own per-conversation platform fees sit on top of Aavartan's price and are outside its control, which compresses what a brand will pay for the intelligence layer.

Regulation bears on the product in three ways. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act governs the conversation transcripts Aavartan stores and re-sends, and Aavartan's data protection officer takes the view — not universally shared inside the company — that a stored transcript re-injected into a model prompt is a processing activity that must be justified by purpose, and that a user's erasure request must reach it. Refunds move over UPI and card rails through the brand's gateway, so reconciliation errors become the brand's problem with its acquiring bank and, ultimately, a matter of RBI-supervised payment operations. And GST invoicing on refunds means a duplicate refund is not merely a lost ₹4,000; it is a credit note that should not exist.

Aavartan's global exposure is one large account. Al Sadeem Retail Group, a Dubai-headquartered retail group operating across the UAE and Oman, signed in June 2026 for Arabic and English support at ₹2.9 crore annually — 9% of ARR, and the reference the New Jersey sales team uses with North American prospects. Al Sadeem's renewal decision is 30 November.

Section 4What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

The original Bolchaal, shipped in March 2025, ran against a 32,000-token window. Because the window was small, the team had built a summariser: after every four turns, a cheaper model compressed the conversation so far into a compact state — the customer's order ID, what had been established, what had been promised, what had been done. That summariser was, in retrospect, the most important component in the system, and nobody thought of it as anything but a workaround for a small window.

In November 2025 the provider's Mumbai region got the 200,000-token model. Vikram Salunke's platform team removed the summariser in the same release. The reasoning was recorded in the pull request and is entirely coherent: the summariser lost detail, generated its own errors, cost a second model call per four turns, and existed only because of a constraint that no longer bound. With 200,000 tokens available and a median conversation of six turns, the whole transcript fitted comfortably. Quality metrics improved. Nobody was wrong on the evidence available.

In February 2026 the team added tools. Bolchaal could now call the brand's order-management system, the courier's tracking API and the payment gateway's refund endpoint. Tool results are returned into the conversation and become part of the prompt on every subsequent turn. A courier tracking response for a multi-item order runs 3,000 to 19,000 tokens of JSON. Nobody capped it, and the pull request that removed the summariser had also removed the token cap that had been guarding the assembly step, because with a 200k window the cap had started firing on legitimate conversations and had been read as a false positive.

What has since turned out to be wrong is not one belief but four. The belief that the median conversation is representative: it is six turns, but the ninety-fifth percentile is forty-one, and the tail is where refunds happen, because the customers who escalate to a refund are the ones who have already tried three other things. The belief that Arabic behaves like English: Al Sadeem's Arabic conversations consume 2.3 times the tokens per message. The belief that the quality evaluation covered production: Shreya Kulkarni's evaluation suite in Toronto was built in early 2025 on conversations averaging eleven turns and has never been rebuilt. And the belief that a 200,000-token window makes truncation impossible: on 22 September, a finance analyst at Rasavati Naturals, a personal-care brand, found 412 duplicate refunds totalling ₹18.4 lakh issued between 8 and 19 September. In every one, the conversation had exceeded roughly fifty turns; the assembly step had silently dropped the oldest messages to fit; and the dropped messages included the tool result recording that a refund had already been issued. Bolchaal, asked again whether a refund would be given, checked what it could see, found no refund, and issued one.

Section 5The people

Ira Bhattacharya, Chief Product Officer, Bengaluru. Position: she has not stated one, which two of her reports have started to read as weakness. Incentive: she owns both the Al Sadeem renewal and the festival readiness plan, and she is the executive who signed off the November 2025 release. What she is not saying: she does not think the company can do anything meaningful in thirteen days, and she suspects the honest answer to the board is that the product has been quietly out of control since February.

Vikram Salunke, VP Engineering, Pune. Position: rebuild context management properly — a state store, a summariser, tool-output pruning, per-turn token budgets — a ten-week programme he calls "context engineering". Incentive: the programme requires four hires he has been trying to get approved since June. Not saying: his team removed the token cap in February without a design review, and his ten-week estimate assumes those hires start immediately.

Renu Chandrasekhar, CFO, Bengaluru. Position: move all volume to the provider's smaller, cheaper model immediately; the quality difference, she says, is "a rounding error compared to the margin". Incentive: the Series C process opens in January, and the provider contract is renegotiated in the same month. Not saying: she has already shown a prospective lead investor a model with 68% gross margin in the fourth quarter, and Exhibit 3's numbers are the ones in it.

Daniel Ostermann, design lead, Berlin. Position: cap conversations at twelve turns and hand off to a human, with a graceful transition. Incentive: he is measured on customer satisfaction, which is highest in short conversations. Not saying: he thinks an autonomous agent should not have refund authority at all and has said so privately to Ira twice, but not in any forum where Naresh would hear it.

Shreya Kulkarni, senior data scientist, Toronto. Position: nothing should be decided until there is an evaluation built on the real distribution of conversation lengths, which she estimates at three weeks. Incentive: professional; she flagged the eval gap in April in a document that received no comments. Not saying: she has an offer from a firm in Waterloo and will decide by the end of October.

Wei-Lin Goh, customer success lead, Singapore. Position: Arabic quality and a written refund-accuracy commitment must be delivered before 30 November or Al Sadeem walks. Incentive: her variable pay is tied to net revenue retention. Not saying: Al Sadeem has been running a four-week pilot with another vendor since mid-September, which Fatima mentioned to her in passing and which she has not put in writing.

Naresh Pillai, head of sales, Newark, New Jersey. Position: freeze everything until 20 November. Incentive: two North American D2C accounts worth a combined ₹4.6 crore are in final procurement. Not saying: one of them has written into its security schedule that "no conversation history shall be truncated or summarised without user notice", a clause he accepted without escalating because he read it as boilerplate.

Arun Menon, data protection officer, Mumbai. Position: the stored-and-re-injected transcript is personal data and the company cannot currently honour an erasure request against material already in flight; he wants processing minimised on principle. Incentive: he is personally named in the company's DPDP filings. Not saying: he has not yet told the board that the Al Sadeem contract's UAE data flows were never reviewed against the same standard the nineteen Indian contracts were.

Section 8The options as Ira currently sees them

Option 1 — Move to the global endpoint and the one-million-token window

Truncation stops being possible for almost all conversations, Arabic fits comfortably, and the newer model families become available. It breaks the in-India data commitment in nineteen contracts, which means either a renegotiation Ira cannot complete before the festival or a two-tier deployment that doubles the operational surface. Cost per conversation rises with prompt length, not falls.

Option 2 — Vikram's ten-week context-engineering programme

Restore a summariser, add a state store outside the prompt, prune tool outputs, impose per-turn token budgets, and make truncation an explicit policy rather than a library default. Addresses the refund mechanism and the cost tail together. Requires four hires under a hiring freeze, and ten weeks from today lands on 13 December — after the festival, after the Al Sadeem decision, and after the North American procurements close.

Option 3 — Cap conversations and hand off to humans

Daniel's Arm C. Ships in under two weeks, caps the cost tail mechanically, and Exhibit 5 says satisfaction improves. It also concedes the autonomy claim that differentiates Bolchaal from every ticketing product in the market, requires brands to staff humans during the festival fortnight when they least can, and rests on an exhibit whose response rates are confounded.

Ira had written all three on a page, and had then written, underneath, a sentence she had not shown anyone: all three of these are answers to "how big should the window be", and the refund happened because a fact about the world was living in a prompt instead of in a database. Nobody at Rasavati would have cared how long the conversation was if the refund service had refused to issue a second refund against the same order. That was a fifteen-line change, and it was not on anyone's list, because the incident had been classified as an AI incident and routed to the platform team. She was not sure whether that observation dissolved the strategic question or merely postponed it, and she was aware that it would sound, at nine in the morning, like a way of avoiding the strategic question entirely.

Section 9The deadline and the hard constraints

The code freeze begins on 12 October and runs to 12 November; it has been in place for two festival seasons and Naresh regards it as inviolable. The provider's minimum commitment of ₹1.1 crore a month runs to January 2027, so a design that cuts token consumption by 60% would take Aavartan below the floor and forfeit the 40% discount on the volume it does use — which means aggressive efficiency is worth less than the arithmetic suggests until the contract is renegotiated. Nineteen contracts carry the in-India data clause. One North American security schedule, already signed by Naresh, forbids undisclosed truncation or summarisation, which arguably rules out both Option 2 and the current behaviour. The hiring freeze holds until the Series C closes. Al Sadeem decides on 30 November. Rasavati's finance team has asked for a written root-cause note and a commitment by 10 October, and the ₹18.4 lakh has been credited back by Aavartan as a goodwill gesture that Renu has not yet booked.

Section 10Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly is in the prompt on turn 47 of the conversation in Exhibit 2, and what is not? Describe the mechanism of the duplicate refund without using the word "model".
  2. Exhibits 3, 4, 5 and 6 each contain a methodological choice that shapes the conclusion a reader draws. Identify the choice in each and say which direction it biases the reader.
  3. Vikram says the November 2025 decision to remove the summariser was correct on the evidence available at the time. Is he right? What evidence, obtainable then, would have changed it?
  4. Renu's proposal is to change models; Daniel's is to change the interaction; Vikram's is to change the architecture. Which of the three, if any, addresses the cause identified in Exhibit 2 — and what does it mean that all three are being argued as responses to the same incident?
  5. Ira's unshown sentence claims the refund failure is a state problem, not a context problem. If she is right, what else in Bolchaal is currently being held in a prompt that ought to be held somewhere else — and what would it cost to find out before 17 October?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Ira do first, what does she tell the board, and what does she tell Fatima Al Suwaidi, Naresh's two prospects, and Rasavati's finance team — given that those four audiences cannot all be told the same thing without one of them hearing something Ira would rather they did not?

The rain had stopped by half past one. Ira closed the finance model, opened the incident report again, and read the timestamp on turn 47 for the fourth time. Somewhere in Pune, Vikram was still awake; she could see him typing in the platform channel and then stopping. She had thirteen days until the peak, nine hours until the board, and no version of the story that was both true and short.
